newsitem.title: FRANCE: Chirac faces battle after left wins French round.
newsitem.headline: Chirac faces battle after left wins French round.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac faces a battle to rescue his centre-right coalition after the opposition left won the first round of a snap parliamentary election he called to seek a "new elan" for his European policy.

Voters sent Chirac a severe warning on Sunday, giving the combined left a 4.5-point lead over the coalition and raising the prospect that the Gaullist president may have to share power with a hostile, Socialist-led government after next Sunday's decisive runoff ballot.

The protest vote against two years of austerity, high taxes and rising unemployment left the second round wide open, putting pressure on Chirac to intervene in the campaign again and possibly dump unpopular Prime Minister Alain Juppe.

With most votes counted in metropolitan France, the Interior Ministry said the combined left had polled 40.1 percent, the RPR-UDF coalition and other right-wing candidates 36.5 percent and the extreme-right National Front 15 percent. Ecologists scored 6.8 percent.
"Chirac's tactical dissolution is turning into a strategic disaster," said constitutional law professor Olivier Duhamel.

The risk of a left-wing victory pushed the deutschemark up against several European currencies in Sunday night trading. Economists forecast a nervous reaction to the left's strong showing when French financial markets open on Monday.

The left pledged vigorous state job-creation measures and a shorter working week without loss of pay to attack record 12.8 percent unemployment. The coalition promised market reforms to scale down state control, cut taxes and free private enterprise.
Sociologist Alain Tourraine compared France to a donkey resisting being dragged towards free-market solutions and suspicious of the planned single European currency.

"The donkey is digging its heels in and doesn't want to go where it is being taken. But it doesn't say where it wants to go," he said. "Public opinion is telling (Chirac) 'you didn't keep your promises and we don't want this policy which leads to more unemployment'."
Juppe, whose unpopularity was a key factor, sought to put a brave face on his side's mediocre result and brushed aside a call to step down for the good of the coalition.
"The French people meant above all to say that they want a real change. We must listen to this message." he said.
When a grassroots activist in Bordeaux asked him whether he should not resign for the sake of the party, he replied: "This is not a fairground and we are not playing musical chairs."

Like Juppe, most cabinet ministers and centre-right leaders were forced into runoffs in their constituencies, some such as ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing and Paris mayor Jean Tiberi for the first time in their parliamentary careers.

Coalition leaders described the vote as a "warning" and said the right must heed the voters' message, but none called openly for Chirac to jettison Juppe or promise a different prime minister to secure a conservative victory.
Socialist party leader Lionel Jospin, sounding more cautious than his cheering supporters, said the vote showed a left-wing majority was possible and urged the left to unite for victory.
He challenged Juppe to a face-to-face television debate but rejected the right's call for a four-party debate that would force him to appear alongside Communist chief Robert Hue.
Hue, whose party could end up holding the balance of power, said Chirac had sought a vote of confidence and the French people had told him "No!".
Most of the 577 National Assembly seats were set to go to a runoff, where the behaviour of National Front supporters and of the 31.6 percent of voters who abstained will be crucial.
The outcome may hinge on the 22 seats in France's overseas departments and territories. Polling stations were still open in the Caribbean and South America long after they closed in Paris.

The BVA polling institute projected the RPR-UDF would win 250 to 270 seats in the runoff, well short of the 289 required for a majority. It gave the Socialists 250-280, the Communists 17-23 and the National Front at most one.

The SOFRES polling firm forecast that the coalition would win 255-287 seats next Sunday. It projected the Socialists would win 242-272 seats, their Communist allies 21-30 seats and the National Front 0-3 seats.
The projections covered only the 555 seats in metropolitan France. Most of the seats in overseas territories were held by centre-right members in the outgoing Assembly.
Chirac gambled his presidency after two years in office on the snap poll, 10 months before his giant parliamentary majority needed to face voters.

The president intervened twice in the campaign for the first round, once to attack the Socialists' record and policies, and the second time to declare solemnly that France needed to speak with a single voice in Europe.

He will have another chance to use the international stage on Monday and Tuesday, when he plays host to Russian President Boris Yeltsin and U.S. President Bill Clinton for a summit to sign the "Founding Act" of a new NATO-Russia partnership.
